scope_note: Curated, source-checked paraphrases from the complete IBO global reports for 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, whose reuse-with-attribution terms were verified. Statements describe reported regional practice, events and constraints; they are not field observations, model output, forecasts or recommendations for this location. Reported losses are industry estimates. Repeated mentions across editions share one source family and are not independent confirmation.
coverage_note: Partial coverage: only selected benchmark regions and countries are included, and only statements checked against the cited pages. Absence of a record is not evidence that an event did not occur or that a practice is not used. The 2021 and 2022 editions and other sources are not included.

records.title: British Columbia heat during bloom, mid-May 2023, cut the crop
records.summary: IBO 2024 reports a cool early spring in British Columbia that delayed bloom until May in many regions. Abnormally hot weather came on suddenly in mid-May, with daily maximum temperatures above 30°C for a few days, and pollination was severely impacted. Bloom became very concentrated, and pollination experts link the heat to poor fruit set and small fruit. The summer was then dry. Levies indicate a 2023 crop of 104 million pounds, a drop of nearly 39%.

records.summary: IBO 2025 states that in 2024 Peruvian producers delayed pruning to capitalize on shortages at the start of that year, after the 2023 El Niño, prompting another delayed start to the season. records.title: El Niño 2023 production shock in Peru
records.summary: IBO 2025 says the 2023 El Niño supply shock upended global markets; Ventura proved especially susceptible to extreme temperatures, and Lima and departments further south were less affected. IBO 2026 says the worst effects were in varieties that were not truly zero-chill, which struggled with bud and flower differentiation in the heat, while fruit grown further south performed better. IBO 2024 also says truly no-chill varieties bred for heat fared better than low-chill ones, and that industry consensus put Biloxi and Ventura among the worst affected, though Ventura did better on some farms. IBO 2024 and 2025 country tables give production of 299.67 thousand t in 2022/23 and 233.87 thousand t in 2023/24.
records.crop_context: Southern highbush; Ventura named as susceptible; true zero-chill evergreen varieties reported to fare well.
limitations: National production change combines weather, area and management; it is not a local loss rate.

records.summary: IBO 2024 reports, from ProArándanos, that in 2023 the El Niño phenomenon and Cyclone Yaku significantly lifted minimum temperatures. This altered the plants' phenological cycles and hit blueberry production. The effect was most evident in the northern region, where varieties that need more cold hours had large falls in production. ProArándanos also says El Niño brought high temperatures year-round, which affected fruit production and export volumes.

records.title: Peru April-May 2023: heat drove strong vegetative growth, an early sign of a short crop
records.summary: IBO 2024 says many stakeholders knew a short season was likely around April and May 2023. By then vegetative growth was much more pronounced than in previous years because of hot conditions, which generally means less fruit. The report adds that the industry was too young to understand an El Niño with such prolonged warm temperatures. The industry trends section names one reason the impact was so severe: reliance on certain public varieties that tend to revert to vegetative growth instead of fruit growth in hot conditions.

records.summary: IBO 2024 says the negative effects of El Niño on Peruvian blueberry fields in 2023 varied with geography, altitude and variety. Growers with proprietary genetics bred for heat tolerance, and most growers in southern Peru, had largely stable production while national volume fell.
records.crop_context: Commercial blueberries; proprietary genetics bred for heat tolerance fared better.

The window is given for northern Namibia as a whole, not for a named farm.

records.title: Northern Namibia: inland sites chosen for fewer frosts, water and labour
records.summary: IBO 2024 reports that Namibia's coastal areas are known for frosts, so the leading northern projects near Rundu, Divundu and the Caprivi Strip are inland where frosts have historically been less common. Growers chose these sites for that, for better access to water and for plentiful labour, over the better logistics of the coast.
records.crop_context: Not specified.
limitations: Regional industry report, not an observation at this map point or farm.
Lower frost prevalence is historical; the same page reports a severe frost in 2023 (see na-kavango-frost).

records.title: Northern NSW floods and wet 2021/22 season
records.summary: IBO 2023 relays the Australian growers' association (ABGA) report that 2021/22 was extremely wet after two La Niñas, with two major floods in Northern NSW, the dominant region. They were not at harvest, but growers could not reach orchards for crop protection, causing significant pest and disease losses; national tonnage fell 16% to 19,600 t.
records.crop_context: Southern highbush and rabbiteye; not specified for losses.
limitations: Geographic scope is Northern NSW, not the whole state.
The 16% fall is national; ABGA and IBO table values differ (19,600 t vs 18.21 thousand t).

records.title: Northern NSW (Coffs Harbour): August-November concentration
records.summary: IBO 2025 says Australian supply is heavily concentrated in August-November from Coffs Harbour, estimated at 75-80% of national volume, with rabbiteye in summer. IBO 2024 also reports the August-November concentration with Coffs Harbour planting behind much of the growth. IBO 2023 says Coffs Harbour has been beset by weather troubles for several years, driving diversification.

period.label: Season pattern described in IBO 2023, 2024 and 2025

records.crop_context: Low-chill southern highbush; rabbiteye in summer.
limitations: Coffs Harbour is in northern NSW; the state match is broader.
Later IBO editions share authors and contributor networks; repeated mentions are not independent confirmation.

records.title: Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred, March 2025
records.summary: IBO 2025 reports that Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred, unusually far south, made landfall at Moreton Bay in March 2025, bringing heavy rain and flooding in southern Queensland and northern NSW; timing was fortunate but caused a later start and higher pest and disease pressure.
records.crop_context: Southern highbush.
limitations: Affected southern Queensland and northern NSW, not the whole states.
Unquantified.

records.title: Western Australia: pruning spreads harvest from March to January
records.summary: IBO 2025 reports the farms of one Western Australia-based breeder, between Gingin and Manjimup, using pruning and farm methods to fill gaps, with harvest from March to January of the following year. IBO 2023 describes the area as dry and Mediterranean with fewer pests, and IBO 2024 as dry with fewer pest pressures.
records.crop_context: Southern highbush; machine-harvest genetics.
limitations: Regional industry report, not an observation at this map point or farm.
IBO 2025 describes one breeder's farms, not all Western Australian growers.

records.title: Australia 2023: return to more normal weather after extreme years
records.summary: IBO 2024 reports, from the Australian Blueberry Growers Association, that 2023 saw a return to more 'normal' conditions after a few years of extreme weather, and yields were up considerably. Production from July 2023 to April 2024 was up 30.9% on the year before. The report team says quality was reportedly much higher.

records.crop_context: Not specified.

National statement; the registry has no Australia country geography, so it is attached to the three state geographies.
The 30.9% rise is a national production change, not a state figure.

records.title: Far North Queensland targets the March to May window
records.summary: IBO 2024 says Far North Queensland, around the Atherton Tablelands and the drier area to its west, has emerged as a growing region that targets the March to May window, though volumes are limited. At least two major breeders are trialling or commercializing varieties there. Queensland also has a large operation in Mundubbera and smaller farms around Bundaberg.
records.crop_context: Not specified; new varieties under trial by breeding companies.
limitations: Regional industry report, not an observation at this map point or farm.
Volumes are described as limited; the window applies to Far North Queensland, not the whole state.

records.title: Nambucca Valley plantings aim to extend the NSW window
records.summary: IBO 2024 says growers are exploring geographic diversification to supply outside the August to November peak. The Nambucca Valley, south of Coffs Harbour, has recent plantings targeting a slight window extension.
records.crop_context: Not specified.
limitations: Regional industry report, not an observation at this map point or farm.
The size of the window extension is not given.

records.title: Waikato frost, October 2022
records.summary: IBO 2023 reports an October 2022 frost from a polar blast that especially hit rabbiteye; helicopters and overhead watering could do little. Waikato, about 40% of the crop, was hit worst; Hawke's Bay and Tauranga less. IBO 2025 recalls that two seasons earlier a bad frost wiped out a significant portion of production.
records.crop_context: Rabbiteye especially affected.
limitations: Text extraction of the 2023 page is column-spliced; attribution checked at medium confidence.
Losses are compounded with later floods; no frost-only figure.

records.title: Hawke's Bay floods and Cyclone Gabrielle, January-February 2023
records.summary: IBO 2023 reports floods in late January to early February 2023 and then Cyclone Gabrielle in February, with Hawke's Bay most affected by waterlogging, disease, submerged farms and wind damage to tunnels. Surveys found growers saying they had probably only 15% of usual production in the compound season.
records.crop_context: Blueberries including tunnelled production.
limitations: 15% refers to growers' survey statements about the whole season, not this event alone.
The source says floods in late January to early February 2023 and Cyclone Gabrielle in February; the stored start and end dates approximate those words and are not exact event dates.

records.title: New Zealand 2024/25: warm spring, then late-summer heat and dry
records.summary: IBO 2025 reports that a warm late winter and early spring 2024 in Waikato and Hawke's Bay advanced maturity, a North Island run of 28 days above 27°C followed, and under-irrigated late varieties shrivelled; some March harvests were a fraction of normal.
records.crop_context: Late varieties on farms without irrigation reserves most affected.
limitations: Regional industry report, not an observation at this map point or farm.
Irrigation access determined impact.

Conflict between sources: the BBNZ summary on IBO 2025 p.159 calls 2024/25 a season of relative calm climatic conditions without major weather impacts, while the report team narrative on p.160 describes the heat and dry losses.

records.title: New Zealand season: peak November-May
records.summary: IBO 2025 describes a main domestic season from November, peaking November-May, with southern highbush in the north targeting August-October and rabbiteye exports mostly February-April. IBO 2024 also describes southern highbush planted for the August-October window. IBO 2024 and 2026 note Hawke's Bay greenhouse production to end of May, while frosts earlier in May end the season for many others.

period.label: Season pattern described in IBO 2024, 2025 and 2026

records.crop_context: Southern highbush (north), rabbiteye, and PNW-type varieties in the South Island.
limitations: Country-level industry context; it does not establish the system, cultivar or timing at this map point.

records.title: New Zealand 2023/24: mild, fairly dry season with high yields
records.summary: IBO 2024 reports that the 2023/24 New Zealand season was mild and reasonably dry, in contrast with the frost, floods and Cyclone Gabrielle of the prior season. Many growers reported their highest yields ever in some blocks. Less rain meant lower disease pressure and more marketable fruit, but invertebrate pest pressure increased. A source called it a 'stellar season' in Waikato and Hawke's Bay.
records.crop_context: Not specified.
limitations: Regional industry report, not an observation at this map point or farm.
The 'stellar season' description comes from one source.
Yield gains are reported by growers for some blocks; no figures are given.

records.title: New Zealand: grower numbers fell after major weather events
records.summary: IBO 2024 reports Blueberries New Zealand figures of 68 growers and 5 exporting groups, against 125 growers and 9 exporting groups in 2023. BBNZ says the major weather events can likely be the cause of the large drop off of growers. The prior season had intensive frost, flooding and Cyclone Gabrielle.

records.crop_context: Not specified.
limitations: Country-level industry context; it does not establish the system, cultivar or timing at this map point.

The counts are BBNZ membership figures; the date of the 68-grower figure is not stated.

records.title: New Zealand: February-May peak, nearly year-round supply
records.summary: IBO 2024 says New Zealand's peak production runs from February to May. Through agronomic techniques, variety choice and growing from Northland to Southland, the country is approaching year-round supply when weather allows, with a dip in June-July. Northland operations can start limited volumes in late June or early July.
records.crop_context: Southern highbush in the north; PNW-type varieties in the South Island.
limitations: Country-level industry context; it does not establish the system, cultivar or timing at this map point.
The peak months differ from IBO 2025, which gives a November-May peak; see the nz-harvest record.
Year-round supply depends on weather conditions, as the text states.

records.title: New Zealand growth from tunnel-grown southern highbush
records.summary: IBO 2024 says much of New Zealand's growth comes from relatively new plantings of premium southern highbush grown under tunnels. Growth is concentrated in the northern North Island, where fruit can be produced earlier.
records.crop_context: Southern highbush under tunnels, several genetics providers.
limitations: Country-level industry context; it does not establish the system, cultivar or timing at this map point.
No tunnel area or share is given.

records.title: India: mid-February to early June season before monsoon
records.summary: IBO 2023, 2024 and 2025 describe India as tropical/subtropical with summer monsoons, mainly low-chill southern highbush with cultivar choice and agronomy used to avoid heavy rain, and a main season from mid-February to early June; protected systems are used for pest pressure.
records.crop_context: Low-chill southern highbush, often protected.
limitations: Country-level industry context; it does not establish the system, cultivar or timing at this map point.
No consensus on best regions is reported.
